summary: Defines the DNAME resource record, which maps an entire subtree of the DNS name space to another domain. It was replaced by RFC 6672.

plainLanguage.summary: DNAME is a DNS record that points a whole branch of the name space at another domain. Any lookup for a name under the branch gets the branch's name swapped for the target, so a subtree can be moved without writing a record for every name in it.

questions: how does dname differ from cname
how does a server process a dname
subtitle: A DNS record that redirects a whole subtree of names to another domain, rather than one name at a time.

tldr.problem: A CNAME record redirects one name, so moving a whole subtree meant writing a CNAME for every name in it, and any name under the moved subtree that already existed would break.
tldr.mechanism: The DNAME record maps an owner name to a target, and any name below the owner has that owner's suffix replaced by the target. The node holding a DNAME may hold other data, but no data may exist at any descendant of it.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2672 was a Proposed Standard. It has since been obsoleted by RFC 6672.

today: RFC 2672 was a Proposed Standard published in August 1999. It has since been obsoleted by RFC 6672.

sections.title: What DNAME Does
sections.content:
The RFC defines a DNS resource record called DNAME, which maps an entire subtree of the DNS name space to another domain. It differs from the CNAME record, which maps a single node of the name space.

The record and its processing rules were conceived as a solution to the problem of maintaining address-to-name mappings in a context of network renumbering. Without the DNAME mechanism, an authoritative DNS server for the address-to-name mappings of some network must be reconfigured when that network is renumbered. With DNAME, the zone can be constructed so that it needs no modification when renumbered. The RFC also notes that DNAME can be useful in other situations, such as when an organizational unit is renamed.
sections.plainLanguage: CNAME moves one name. DNAME moves a branch of names at once, which is what makes it useful when a network is renumbered or an organisation changes its domain.

sections.title: The DNAME Resource Record
sections.content:
The DNAME record has the mnemonic DNAME and type code 39 in decimal, and its format is <owner> <ttl> <class> DNAME <target>. The format is not class-sensitive and all fields are required; the RDATA field, the target, is a domain name. The DNAME record causes type NS additional section processing.

The effect of the record is the substitution of the record's target for its owner as a suffix of a domain name. A no-descendants limitation governs the use of DNAMEs in a zone file: if a DNAME record is present at a node, there may be other data at that node, except a CNAME or another DNAME, but there must be no data at any descendant of that node. This restriction applies only to records of the same class as the DNAME record.

The rule assures predictable results when a DNAME record is cached by a server which is not authoritative for the record's zone, and it must be enforced when authoritative zone data is loaded. Together with the rules for DNS zone authority it implies that DNAME and NS records can only coexist at the top of a zone which has only one node.

The compression scheme of the DNS specification must not be applied to the RDATA portion of a DNAME record unless the sending server knows that the receiver understands the DNAME record format; signalling such understanding is expected to be the subject of future DNS extensions. Naming loops can be created with DNAME records, or a combination of DNAME and CNAME records, just as they can with CNAME records alone, so resolvers, including resolvers embedded in DNS servers, must limit the resources they devote to any query. Implementors should note, however, that fairly lengthy chains of DNAME records may be valid.
sections.plainLanguage: A DNAME sits at the top of a branch and names the branch's new home. Nothing may exist below it, which keeps the redirection unambiguous, and the target must not be compressed on the wire.

sections.title: Query Processing
sections.content:
To use the DNAME mechanism the name resolution algorithms must be modified slightly for both servers and resolvers. Both modified algorithms incorporate the operation of making a substitution on a name, either the query name or the server name, under the control of a DNAME record, and this is called the DNAME substitution.

For a server performing non-recursive service, the matching process changes to check for a DNAME record before checking for a wildcard label. When the match fails at some label, the server looks to see whether the last label matched has a DNAME record. If it does, the record is copied into the answer section; if the substitution would overflow the legal size for a domain name, the response code is set to YXDOMAIN, otherwise the substitution is performed and the search starts again.

DNS clients sending Extended DNS queries with version 0, and non-extended queries, are presumed not to understand the semantics of the DNAME record. A server implementing this specification, when answering such a query, should synthesize a CNAME record for each DNAME record encountered during query processing, to help the client reach the correct DNS data. The synthesized CNAME must have the same CLASS as the QCLASS of the query, a TTL of zero, an owner equal to the query name in effect at the moment the DNAME record was encountered, and an RDATA field containing the new query name formed by the DNAME substitution. If the server has the appropriate key on line, it may generate and return a signature for the synthesized CNAME.

A resolver or a server providing recursive service must treat a DNAME as somewhat analogous to a CNAME. When the response shows a DNAME and that is not the answer itself, the resolver caches the DNAME, checks whether the substitution would overflow the legal size for a domain name, and if not performs the substitution and starts again. A resolver that understands DNAME records but sends non-extended queries must delete from the reply any CNAME records whose owner is a subdomain of the owner of any DNAME record in the response.
sections.plainLanguage: When a lookup reaches a DNAME, the server swaps the branch's name for the target and starts the search again. Older clients that do not know about DNAME get a synthesized CNAME instead, so they still arrive at the right answer.

sections.title: Examples of Use
sections.content:
For an organisational renaming, if an organisation with domain name FROBOZZ.EXAMPLE became part of an organisation with domain name ACME.EXAMPLE, it might ease transition by placing a record such as this in its old zone:

frobozz.example. DNAME frobozz-division.acme.example. MX 10 mailhub.acme.example.

The response to an extended recursive query for www.frobozz.example would then contain, in the answer section, the DNAME record shown above and the relevant records for www.frobozz-division.acme.example.

For classless delegation of shorter prefixes, the classless scheme for in-addr.arpa delegation can be extended to prefixes shorter than 24 bits by using the DNAME record. The prefix 192.0.8.0/22 can be delegated with an NS record for 8/22 in the zone 0.192.in-addr.arpa and DNAME records pointing at 8.8/22, 9.8/22, 10.8/22 and 11.8/22. A typical entry in the resulting reverse zone for a host with address 192.0.9.33 is a PTR record for 33.9 in the zone 8/22.0.192.in-addr.arpa.

For network renumbering support, the RFC shows a chain of DNAME records in the new-style.in-addr.arpa zone and the in-addr.example.net zone that would allow the address space 190.189.0.0/16 assigned to one provider to be changed without altering the zone files describing the use of that space by the provider and its customers. The RFC notes that renumbering IPv4 networks is so arduous that updating the DNS is only a small part of the labour, so the scheme may have low value, but it is hoped that the task will be different in IPv6 and the DNAME mechanism may play a useful part.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC gives three worked uses: renaming an organisation, delegating a reverse zone for a prefix shorter than 24 bits, and moving an address block without rewriting the zone files of everyone using it.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: The document defines a new DNS resource record type with the mnemonic DNAME and type code 39 in decimal. The naming and numbering space is defined in the DNS specification, and this name and number have already been registered with IANA.
sections.plainLanguage: DNAME was allocated the DNS type code 39.
